activity: to use loops and if-then blocks in Scratch to make a game that keeps score
knowledge_domain: to use loops and if-then blocks in Scratch to make a game that keeps score
fact: In Scratch, clicking the green flag starts every script that begins with 'when green flag clicked', and the red stop sign stops all scripts.
story:
Ryan pressed the green flag for the fourth time, and for the fourth time nothing happened. His cat sprite sat frozen in the corner of the stage while the score variable blinked at zero. Around him, the computer lab hummed with other games springing to life, basketballs bouncing and dragons flapping, and Kyleigh two seats over already had a fish dodging sharks.

"It worked yesterday," Ryan muttered. He scrolled through his code. He had the loop set up right, a forever block that moved the cat toward the mouse pointer, and an if-then block that added one to the score whenever the cat touched a coin. Yesterday the cat had chased that coin all over the stage. Today, silence.

Kylan leaned over from the next row. "Did you try the red stop sign?"

"Everything's already stopped. That's the problem." Ryan clicked the stop sign anyway, just to be sure, and the other games in the room kept playing because the stop sign only stopped scripts, not the whole program. Then he sat back and stared at his stack of blocks, starting from the top. Green flag, he thought. Kyleigh's fish moved the second she clicked her flag. Her scripts must all begin with the same block. He scrolled up to his own stack and felt his stomach drop. His forever loop began with a plain blue block, nothing above it. There was no hat block, no rounded yellow block on top saying "when green flag clicked." Yesterday he must have dragged his code out from under it by accident, and clicking the green flag started nothing because no script began with that block. All his fixing had been in vain.

He dragged the hat block back onto the top of his stack and clicked the green flag. The cat sprang to life, streaked toward the coin, and the score jumped from zero to one. He converted the whole game idea right then, deciding he would add a second coin and a timer so the score would actually mean something by Friday.

"That was it?" Kylan said.

"That was it." Ryan saved his file twice, which he now considered his testimony to never trusting a single save again, and watched the cat snatch the coin for the fifth time. "Kyleigh, do you have an extra coin sprite I can borrow?"

activity: to explain supply and demand using the price of strawberries in summer and winter
knowledge_domain: to explain supply and demand using the price of strawberries in summer and winter
fact: Where strawberries ripen outdoors in early summer, a flood of local berries raises the supply all at once, which usually pushes their price down.
story:
Riley stared at the flyer Mr. Munro had taped to the classroom door. "Market Project," it read. "Explain why something costs what it costs." Everyone else had already picked easy things like video games or sneakers, but Riley wanted the thing that had bugged him since Saturday: at the market with his mom, strawberries had cost half what they cost in March. He'd seen the March price himself, four dollars a basket, and now the same basket was two.

"You should do it," said Kaiya at lunch. "You're the one who kept saying 'but why' in the produce aisle until your mom walked away."

"It's like there's a hidden rule," Riley said. "Prices don't just happen. Something invisible is moving them."

After school, he and Wilson stood at the corner where a farm truck parked every June. The farmer was stacking basket after basket of red berries, more than anyone could eat in a week. Riley counted the baskets out of curiosity and got to sixty before Wilson elbowed him.

"Ask him," Wilson whispered.

"Do these all ripen around now?" Riley asked.

"Early summer, all at once," the farmer said. "The whole valley's berries come in together."

Riley wrote that in his notebook. The word that came to him was supply. In March there were barely any strawberries, and in June the supply flooded in. Maybe price went the opposite way? He drew a see-saw in his notebook: supply up, price down. It was only a guess, though. He wanted proof.

So he made a chart. March: four dollars, few berries. April: three fifty. June: two dollars, baskets everywhere. He taped the chart to a poster and stood in front of the class, holding up a drawing of the farmer's loaded truck.

"Supply is how much of something there is to buy," Riley said. "And where strawberries ripen outdoors in early summer, the local berries all arrive at once, so the supply jumps up, and that usually pushes the price down."

"Usually?" said Mr. Munro, one eyebrow up.

"Prices are turbulent," Riley said. "They wobble. One market could still charge more, for a day or so. But the pattern held every month I checked." He paused. "Here's what I still wonder. When summer ends and the berries cease coming, do prices climb back up slowly, or jump? I want to keep a chart through the winter."

Kaiya raised her hand. "Can I help?"

Riley grinned and slid the empty October page across the desk toward her.

activity: to put a bandage on a cut and know when a wound needs a doctor
knowledge_domain: to put a bandage on a cut and know when a wound needs a doctor
fact: A thin layer of petroleum jelly or antibiotic ointment keeps a cut's surface moist, which helps it heal and can reduce scarring.
story:
Louis was sliding the last wet quilt into the dryer when the metal lip of the machine caught his knuckle and opened a line of skin that welled red. He hissed and held his hand over the folding table while Elora, who had come along to keep him company, dug through her backpack.

"You have to let it dry out," she said, tearing a paper towel from the dispenser on the wall. "My grandpa says air is the best thing for a cut."

"That makes a scab, though," Louis said. He was thinking of his elbow from last summer, a scrape he had picked at for weeks, and how it had left a pale mark. There was something he could not see directly here, some rule about how skin fixed itself, and he wanted to find it. He turned the paper towel over and studied the smear of blood, which was thin, not gushing. "It's not deep. It's not going to need a doctor. But I want to test something."

In the laundromat's cramped office, next to a jar of pens and the coin box that was the whole commerce of the place, he found a small tube labeled petroleum jelly and a box of adhesive bandages. Elora raised her eyebrows. "You're putting grease on it? That's so weird. You're being gullible, believing some old jar."

"Watch," Louis said, and he dabbed a thin layer of the jelly across the cut before pressing on the bandage, smoothing the edges flat. "Grandpa's way keeps it dry. Mine keeps it wet. If I'm wrong, my hand falls off." He said it flat enough that she laughed.

They sat on the counter while the dryer tumbled, and the neighbor who ran the place came by to sweep. Louis showed her his bandaged knuckle and asked, quietly, whether air or jelly was better. She nodded at it. "The jelly keeps the surface moist. That helps it heal, and it can mean less of a scar." Elora made a face, but she pulled out her phone to check, then looked up, defeated.

By the time the quilt came out warm, Louis had peeled back one corner of the bandage to look. The cut was closed at the edges, shiny and clean under its thin coat.

"Fine," Elora said, handing him the next load of quarters. "But if it takes longer to heal and prolongs your hand problem, I get to say I told you so."

"Deal," Louis said, and pressed the corner back down.

activity: going away to summer camp for the first time
knowledge_domain: going away to summer camp for the first time
fact: In the Northern Hemisphere, the two stars at the outer edge of the Big Dipper's bowl, called the pointer stars, point toward Polaris, the North Star.
story:
Gabriel's duffel bag sat on the lakeside dock like it was already boarding a bus without him. Tomorrow he left for two weeks of sleepaway camp, and tonight Martha and Charlotte had dragged him out here for a send-off, which so far meant lying on the rough boards and avoiding the splinters.

Then Charlotte announced her plan. "At camp, when the counselors take your phones the first night, you're going to be helpless. You can't even find north."

"I can find north," Gabriel said.

Martha propped herself up on one elbow. "Prove it. No phone, right now."

Gabriel patted his pockets anyway, out of habit, and felt a jolt of embarrassment when Martha raised an eyebrow at him. He set the phone face down on the dock like a prisoner surrendering a weapon. Above the far shore, the sky had gone properly dark, and there was the Big Dipper, hanging over the water like a giant soup ladle someone had left out.

He remembered something from a library book, half remembered, which was worse than not remembering. The two stars at the outer edge of the Dipper's bowl, the ones called the pointer stars, pointed toward Polaris, the North Star. He found the bowl, traced a line up from those two edge stars with his finger, and landed on a lone, stubbornly bright star. "That's Polaris," he said. "So that's north."

"That's it? One star?" Charlotte squinted. "How do you know it's the right one?"

Gabriel inhaled the cold lake air and considered lying. Instead he picked up a wood chip, set it on the boards, and turned it so its edge lined up with Polaris. "If I'm wrong, we walk toward Canada by accident and become extinct, like the dinosaurs."

Martha stood, marched ten paces in the direction the wood chip pointed, and stopped at the end of the dock. From there you could see the town's water tower, and everyone knew the water tower stood on the north side of the lake.

She turned around slowly. "Huh."

"Told you," Gabriel said, and lay back down on the warm boards to look at the Dipper some more.

activity: to explain how a bill becomes a law by passing through the legislature
knowledge_domain: to explain how a bill becomes a law by passing through the legislature
fact: In the United States, Congress can override a president's veto if two-thirds of both the House and the Senate vote to pass the bill again.
story:
Grandma's kitchen smelled like lemon and burned toast, which meant she had been reading again and forgot the toaster. Clara spread her notes across the table and groaned.

"I have to explain how a bill becomes a law on Monday, and I don't get the part after the veto." Clara pushed the paper toward her grandmother. "The president says no, and that's it, right? Dead bill."

Grandma slid the toast onto a plate and sat down. "Hmm. What does your book say?"

"That Congress can do something if enough of them vote again. But it's a weird number and I always mix it up." Clara squinted at the page. "Two-thirds of both the House and the Senate. Both of them. Not just one."

"Then that's the rule. Want to test it?"

Clara was skeptical. "Test it? It's a rule on paper. You can't poke it."

"Sure you can." Grandma pulled a jar of buttons from the windowsill, the way she did before a game. "We'll be Congress."

Earlier that fall, Clara remembered, she had watched a veteran on the news say that one stubborn senator could obstruct a whole bill by talking forever. She had thought laws were like doors that either opened or stayed shut. Now she wasn't so sure. If enough people pushed, maybe a shut door could open again.

They made the House out of twelve buttons and the Senate out of ten. Grandma was the president. Clara's bill, to make Saturday mornings start an hour later, passed both houses easily the first time, and Grandma vetoed it with a smug little tap of her spoon.

"Okay," Clara said, counting. "Two-thirds of twelve is eight, and two-thirds of ten is almost seven, so I need seven there. I need eight House buttons and seven Senate buttons to vote yes again."

Grandma frowned at the piles like a president should. "That's a lot of buttons."

Clara flipped them one at a time, saying yes for each one. The Senate pile reached seven. The House pile stopped at seven. Eight was needed, and there were only seven, because one button, the blue one, had rolled under the sugar bowl.

"One short," Clara said. "So the veto holds? The bill just dies?"

"In our Congress, yes. Both houses, two-thirds, or the president wins." Grandma fished out the blue button and set it back with the others. "You were wrong this morning, you know. You said a veto was the end."

Clara had changed her own mind right there at the table, and she said so. A veto wasn't the end unless Congress was too small or too split. She copied the rule onto an index card and underlined both twice.

Monday morning, Mr. Fischer called on her first. Clara stood up, took out the buttons, and lined them along the chalk tray.

"Volunteers," she said. "I need twelve of you to be the House."

activity: to shade a sphere with a light source to show highlight, shadow and cast shadow
knowledge_domain: to shade a sphere with a light source to show highlight, shadow and cast shadow
fact: The terminator is the line on a sphere where the lit side turns into the shadow side, the edge where direct light stops reaching.
story:
Zack pushed his desk lamp closer to the orange he had stolen from the fruit bowl, until the light nearly touched the skin. He was supposed to be drawing a sphere for Monday's art assignment, but his last three attempts looked like flat gray circles wearing smudges. He wanted this one to look like it could roll off the page, and he had all afternoon to figure out how.

The orange gave him an idea. He grabbed it and carried it to his dark bathroom, where the only light came from the hallway through a crack in the door. He set the orange on the counter and crouched down until his eyes were level with it. Half of the orange glowed bright orange, and the other half sat in a brown dusk. Between the two halves ran a border, a soft but definite line where the glow simply stopped.

He remembered art class on Friday, when Abigael had laughed out loud at Mr. Korhonen's vocabulary list. "The terminator," Mr. Korhonen had read, tapping the whiteboard. "Who can tell me what that means on a sphere?" Corey had immediately spread his arms like a robot and marched in place, and the whole class cracked up. But then Mr. Korhonen had pointed at the globe in the corner, and Abigael traced her finger around its edge and gone quiet. Zack had squinted at the globe then, but now, in the bathroom, he actually saw it. The terminator was the line on a sphere where the lit side turned into the shadow side, the edge where direct light stopped reaching.

Back at his desk, he sharpened his pencil to a needle point. The bathroom orange had shown him something he had missed before: the terminator was not a sharp fence, it was a soft frontier, and the sphere got darker gradually as it curved away from the lamp. He tested it, laying down short strokes that started light right past the bright spot, the highlight, and stacked them heavier and heavier toward that border. Where the shadow side began, he stopped almost completely, leaving just a whisper of gray because the desk bounced light back up. Then, underneath and to the right, he drew the cast shadow, the dark pool the sphere threw onto the table, darkest near the orange where it touched.

He could smell the orange's sharp peel still on his fingers as he leaned the drawing against his lamp. It looked round. It looked real. He grabbed his phone and texted Abigael a photo, then another text: "No robots were harmed in the making of this terminator." Three dots appeared, then her reply: "Send me your orange trick tomorrow. Mine still looks like a gray cookie." Zack grinned and texted back, "Bring fruit. I have monopoly on the bathroom lab until dinner."

activity: to recognise the warning signs of anxiety in a friend and know who to tell
knowledge_domain: to recognise the warning signs of anxiety in a friend and know who to tell
fact: Anxiety can show up in the body as a racing heart, fast breathing, stomachaches, headaches or trouble sleeping.
story:
Every Saturday, Austin took the bus out to his grandpa's house on the lake, and every Saturday his friend Jad came along. Grandpa liked to say he was a descendant of a lake captain who had rowed mail across these same waters a hundred years ago, and part of the tradition was that whoever visited had to swim off the old wooden dock. Jad always wore his red trunks with the elastic waistband, and every Saturday, somewhere around eleven o'clock, Jad would go quiet, hold his stomach, and announce, "I feel sick. I'm going inside."

Austin started writing it down in the back of his notebook, the way Grandpa tracked the weather. Saturday, stomachache. Saturday, stomachache and headache. He noticed other things too. When they played cards on the porch while they waited for swim time, Jad's heart seemed to pound so hard Austin could almost see it at his collar, and his breathing went quick and shallow, like he'd run the hill. One night they camped in Grandpa's screen tent, and Jad tossed for hours. "I never sleep good on Fridays," he admitted. "Or Saturdays."

Austin had a theory, but he needed proof. The next Saturday it thundered, and nobody swam. Jad ate two grilled cheese sandwiches, won three hands of gin rummy, and laughed until he had to sit down. No stomachache, no headache, nothing. The Saturday after that, the sun blazed, the lake lay flat and shiny, and by eleven o'clock Jad was pale with his hand pressed to his middle. It wasn't the day that made him sick, Austin realized. It was the dock.

"Want to submerge just your feet today?" Austin offered. "Sit on the ladder and that's it." Jad stared at the dark green water below the boards where the minnows swirled. "It's not the water exactly," he said slowly. "It's the jump. Everybody watches. My brother says anxiety means you're scared, but I'm not scared scared. My body just does this stuff anyway."

Austin rowed him ashore and knocked on the screen door of the blue cottage next door, because Ms. Paquette, who was a retired school nurse, knew about this kind of thing. She listened to the notebook being read aloud, all those Saturdays lined up in ink, and nodded. "Bodies send up flares," she said. "Somebody should tell Jad's mom exactly what you told me. That's not tattling, that's the map."

On the bus home, Jad looked out the window for a long moment. "Saturday, I'm going to try the ladder," he said. "And tonight I'm going to tell my mom about the not-sleeping part too." He bumped Austin's shoulder with his fist and grinned. "Bring the notebook. She likes evidence."

activity: to learn a traditional dance or song well enough to perform it at a community gathering
knowledge_domain: to learn a traditional dance or song well enough to perform it at a community gathering
fact: In the Philippine dance tinikling, two people tap bamboo poles on the ground twice and then clap them together on the third beat while dancers step in and out.
story:
Noemie stood at the back of the parish hall in her socks, watching two kids from the older group kneel on the floor with long bamboo poles. The hall smelled like candle wax and old coffee, and through the open door she could hear someone vacuuming the church carpets. In two weeks, dancers from every family in the congregation would perform at the harvest gathering, and Noemie had signed up for tinikling before she understood what it involved.

The poles clattered twice against the floor, then snapped together on the third beat, and the older dancers slid their feet out just in time. "Tap, tap, clap," went the rhythm, over and over, while bare feet stepped in and out. Julia tried first. She lasted four beats before the poles pinched her ankle, and she hopped away laughing, though her eyes looked worried. Adelaide lasted six. When Noemie's turn came, she got pinched on the very first clap.

She sat on the floor to rub her ankle and watched the older kids again. The pattern never changed: the poles hit the ground twice, then closed on the third beat, then the whole thing repeated. The pole players didn't watch the dancers at all; they watched each other, keeping the beat steady like a metronome. Noemie realized she had been watching the poles themselves, which moved too fast to follow. The poles weren't the thing to track. The beat was.

She stood up and went to the middle. "Say the count out loud with me," she told Julia and Adelaide, who had come to hold the poles for her practice. "Tap, tap, clap. Tap, tap, clap." With the words in her mouth, her feet knew exactly when to land between the poles and when to pull out. On the clap beats, her ankles were already clear. She danced eight rounds without a single pinch, and Ms. Campbell-Brown, who was arranging chairs near the folding tables, called out, "Now that's how you negotiate a pair of bamboo poles!"

Fatigue crept in after twenty minutes, and Noemie's counting got slower than the poles, so the second pole player, an eccentric boy who wore a bow tie even to practice, sped up to match her. They grinned at each other.

On the night of the gathering, the hall filled with families and the smell of rice and fried bananas. Noemie took her place, and when the poles began, she heard herself say it, quiet and steady.

"Tap, tap, clap. Tap, tap, clap."

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: U.S. food safety guidelines say poultry is safely cooked when its thickest part reaches 165 degrees Fahrenheit, or about 74 degrees Celsius, measured with a food thermometer.
story:
Tristan held the food thermometer like it was a magic wand, which was a metaphor his dad would probably ruin by saying thermometers are actually tools. Dinner was Tristan's job tonight, his first time cooking the whole meal at the campsite, and he had decided on chicken, foil potatoes, and corn. The chicken was the problem. The fire crackled, indifferent to his plans, flaring up whenever the wind shifted and dying down when it didn't.

"You're staring at that chicken like it's going to talk," said Bowen, who was camping two sites over and had wandered over the moment he smelled food. Ayah trailed behind him, carrying a bag of marshmallows like they were already invited.

"It's not talking," Tristan said. "That's the whole point." He flipped his dad's laminated camp cookbook open to the page he'd read four times. It said poultry was safely cooked when its thickest part reached 165 degrees Fahrenheit, which was about 74 degrees Celsius, measured with a food thermometer. Not guessed from the color. Not poked with a fork. Measured. "My grandpa always said if the juices run clear, it's done. But clear juice is a clue, not a rule."

"So you trust the thermometer more than your grandpa?" Ayah asked, peeking into the skillet.

"I trust it more than my eyes." Tristan slid the probe into the fattest piece, right near the bone where the cookbook said the thickest part would be. The numbers climbed: 140, 150, 158. His stomach growled like a fourth camper. Bowen leaned in so far his marshmallow bag nearly caught fire.

At 163, the reading stopped climbing. Tristan waited, watching the fire spit. He thought about how his grandpa would classify this as wasting time, but Tristan wanted proof, not hope. Ten seconds later the display ticked up: 165.

"Done!" Tristan shouted it so loud a kid at the next campsite looked over. He pulled the chicken off the grate and cut into the biggest piece. Steam curled out, and the meat was white all the way through, cooked and juicy at the same time.

His dad wandered back from the lake with Tristan's little sister, sniffing the air. "Smells official," his dad said. "How'd you know it was ready?"

Tristan held up the thermometer like a trophy. "One hundred sixty-five degrees," he announced. "In the thickest part. That's the rule."

Bowen was already reaching for a piece. "Save me the drumstick, chef."

activity: the idea of a hypothesis as a testable guess that an experiment can support or overturn
knowledge_domain: the idea of a hypothesis as a testable guess that an experiment can support or overturn
fact: A control group is treated exactly like the test group except for the one thing being tested, so any difference can be traced to that change.
story:
Georgia set four basil pots in a row on the kitchen counter, each one wearing a paper label in her careful handwriting. Marco leaned over them, sniffing. "They smell amazing already."

"That's the problem," Georgia said. "I've been giving them the fancy fertilizer every week, and they look great. But Mr. Rao asked me how I know the fertilizer is doing it." She poked a leaf. "Maybe they'd look this good anyway. Maybe it's the sunny window."

Marco pulled a stool over and sat down. "So do half of them without it."

"Then I wouldn't know if it's the fertilizer or just that they're different plants." She turned a pot so its label faced them. Her instinct said the answer was in keeping everything matched, though she couldn't have said why yet. She got out her notebook and started a list: same window, same water, same soil, same size pots.

She stopped, pen hovering. "Wait. If everything is the same except one thing, the fertilizer, then that's the only thing that could make a difference." She drew a line down the page. "Two pots get fertilizer, two don't. Everything else I do exactly the same to all four."

"Like a race where everybody runs the same track," Marco said, "and one kid gets secret shoes."

Georgia laughed. "Sort of. I need a control group. Pots treated exactly like the others except for the one thing I'm testing."

Cordelia arrived with her mom's old measuring cup, because she wanted the basil for a pizza project on Saturday and had been nagging Georgia about the harvest for weeks. "You're not going to slow them down with some experiment, are you? I need authentic fresh basil, not sad little leaves."

"If the fertilizer works, you'll get more," Georgia said. She held the cup under the tap and measured the water twice, once for each side of her line, so every pot got exactly the same amount. Marco wrote the numbers down while she poured.

Cordelia watched the two plain pots, the unfertilized ones, sitting beside their glossy neighbors. "Fine," she said, changing her mind with a shrug. "Do it right. I'd rather wait for real proof than eat mediocre pizza."

"Saturday," Georgia promised, and turned all four pots a quarter turn toward the light.

activity: to explain how sound travels as vibrations and why it moves faster through water than air
knowledge_domain: to explain how sound travels as vibrations and why it moves faster through water than air
fact: A sound's loudness depends on its amplitude, how far the particles move back and forth; bigger vibrations make louder sounds.
story:
Evelyn had one job for the science fair demo: explain how sound travels, and why it moves faster through water than air. She had a drum, a bag of rice, a bucket of water, and a suspicion that Mr. Fitzgerald had assigned this topic specifically because he owned earplugs.

"Hit it soft," she told Ivan, who was holding the drumstick like it might bite.

He tapped the drumhead. The rice on top shivered, barely. Ivan hit it harder, and the rice jumped a full inch, raining down onto the gym floor with a sound like tiny applause. Evelyn leaned in until her nose was almost touching the drum.

"The rice is doing what the air does," she said. "Particles bumping back and forth. Watch the middle of the jump." She drew the arc in the air with her finger. "How far they travel, that's the amplitude. Bigger vibrations, louder sound."

"That's the word," Charlie said from behind the water bucket, where he was supposed to be taking notes and was instead cherishing a rice grain he'd found in his sleeve. "Amplitude. Write it down before you forget it and call it the jumpy distance."

Mr. Fitzgerald wandered over. "You realize you'll be cleaning that rice up."

"It's testimony," Evelyn said, pointing at the floor. "Every grain is evidence of how hard Ivan hit." Then she picked up the tuning fork she'd borrowed from the supply cabinet, struck it against her shoe, and dipped it toward the bucket.

The water erupted. Waves slapped the rim and slopped over Charlie's shoes, and his yelp carried all the way to the far bleachers, where kids doing jump rope turned to look. Evelyn grinned. The smile was infectious; even Charlie, dripping, started to laugh.

"Some of that," she said, "traveled through your shoe water faster than your scream traveled through air. Write that down."

activity: to create a strong password and explain why the same one should not be reused
knowledge_domain: to create a strong password and explain why the same one should not be reused
fact: In credential stuffing, attackers take usernames and passwords leaked from one site and try them automatically on many other sites, so one reused password can unlock several accounts.
story:
Megan sat on the porch of her grandfather's house with her laptop open, refreshing the login page for the fourth time. "It still says my password is wrong," she typed to Foster. "And I didn't change it."

"Did you get that weird email from the pet forum last night?" Foster wrote back. "Somebody leaked their whole list."

Megan stared at the screen. Her pet forum password, the one she'd made when she was nine, was dragon16. Her game account, the one she and Damian needed for tonight's tournament at seven, used the same password because it was easy to remember. She typed dragon16 into her email login just to test the idea, and her stomach dropped when it loaded her inbox. If she could get in with a reused password, so could somebody else. That had to be what happened to the game account. Somebody took the leaked forum passwords and, she reasoned, must have tried them automatically on other sites until one worked. She changed her email password right there, fingers shaking a little.

Mr. Wardak, the neighbour who came over every Tuesday to fix her grandfather's fence, climbed down his ladder and leaned over her shoulder. "You look like you lost a war," he said.

"Somebody took my game account. I used the same password on a forum that got hacked."

Mr. Wardak nodded slowly. "That's called credential stuffing," he said, and went back to his nails.

Megan messaged Damian, who negotiated with the tournament organizer for a ten-minute extension while she emailed the game's support team with proof the account was hers. Then she opened a notebook and started over. Instead of a word she loved, she strung together random letters and numbers, different for every site, and wrote each one down. "You're my password notebook now," she told it, which was easier than admitting she'd never had a system before.

At 6:52, support restored the account. Damian sent a single word: "GO." Megan logged in with her new password, and the tournament screen bloomed open in front of her.

activity: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
knowledge_domain: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
fact: Professional fact-checkers use lateral reading: instead of judging a website by its own pages, they open new tabs to see what other sources say about it.
story:
Sophie tapped the screen so hard the tablet nearly slid off the lab bench. "Look at this. GlowWater says their drink makes you run faster in one week."

Tyrell leaned over her shoulder. "That website looks amazing. Blue water, a doctor in a white coat, stars everywhere."

"Five stars," Maiya said from the next bench. "And a countdown clock. That means it's real, right?"

Mr. Ong was walking between the rows of benches, straightening beakers, but Sophie noticed he slowed down near their table, listening. She scrolled down the site. The doctor had a name, Dr. Harmon, and a quote in big letters. There were photographs of sweaty, happy runners holding blue bottles. Everything about the page wanted her to believe it, and she almost did.

"Here's the thing," she said slowly. "The site can't stop talking about itself. Every page is another page from the same people." She opened a new tab and typed GlowWater into the search bar. The results made her sit back. A newspaper article appeared first: "GlowWater sold by the same company that makes it." Then a runner's blog: "The 'independent study' was run by the company's owner." Then a small item about Dr. Harmon, who turned out to be an actor in a toothpaste ad.

"That's sneaky," Tyrell said. "The whole website is one big ad wearing a costume."

"It's like when the algorithm on my video app keeps feeding me more of the same thing," Maiya said. "Everything agrees because it all comes from one place." Sophie nodded and copied the idea onto her worksheet: don't only read the site, read around it. Later she found a name for it in one of the newspaper articles, and she underlined it twice. "It's called lateral reading," she announced. "Instead of judging a website by its own pages, you open new tabs and see what other sources say about it."

Mr. Ong stopped at their bench. "Whose idea was the new tabs?"

"Mine, but Maiya gave me the extra battery pack when my tablet died halfway," Sophie confessed, "so really it was a team effort."

Maiya grinned and slid the battery pack back into her pencil case. "And Tyrell found the actor. He has a fertile imagination for detective work."

"I found the toothpaste ad in four seconds," Tyrell said. "Someday I will open my own detective agency. GlowWater will be my first case."

activity: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
knowledge_domain: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
fact: In the United States, the cost of crude oil is usually the largest single part of the price of a gallon of gasoline, so pump prices tend to rise when crude oil prices rise.
story:
Sawyer had been watching the same glitter card on the marketplace app for three days, and every morning the price climbed higher. First it was twelve dollars, then fifteen, then twenty-two. There were only two listed, and forty-one people had them in their wish lists. He refreshed the page outside the gas station while his dad filled the tank, and the little red "price increased" tag glowed like a warning light.

"Why did it go up again since last week?" a kid at the next pump asked his own father, pointing at the numbers on the sign. His father shrugged, but Sawyer's dad leaned over. "Crude oil is usually the biggest single part of what a gallon of gas costs," he said. "So when crude oil gets more expensive, pump prices go up too." Sawyer stared at the card on his screen, then at the sign. Scarce thing, lots of people wanting it, price rising. He wondered if the same hidden rule ran both places, though nobody could see it working.

He decided to test it. In his room that evening, luminous desk lamp pulled close, he opened his trade folder. He owned six copies of a card that used to be rare, one he'd once traded his best technique guide to get. For months he had opposed selling them, remembering how hard they were to find. Now there were dozens listed online, and the price had slid from nine dollars to two. He posted three copies at two dollars and watched. Within an hour, two other sellers dropped their prices too. Plentiful thing, price falling. His stomach did a small flip.

The next day he showed the screenshots to Meriem at lunch. "So scarcity pushes prices up, and plenty pushes them down," she said, chewing her sandwich. "Even for gas." Sawyer nodded, though a question still bothered him. He'd sold one card cheap to prove his idea, and now that same card felt harder to let go of than he'd expected. "Think it'll ever get scarce again?" Meriem asked. Sawyer refreshed the app under the table. "Fourteen listed," he said. "Ask me next week."

activity: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
knowledge_domain: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
fact: In Chinese, the word for 'four' sounds very similar to the word for 'death', so some buildings in East Asia skip the fourth floor.
story:
Claire pressed the elevator button for the fourth floor three times before she noticed it wasn't there. The buttons jumped from three to five, like a stair with a missing step. "Wade," she said, "your building's elevator is broken. There's no four."

Wade lived on the eighth floor, above the restaurant his parents owned, and tonight Claire and Andie were coming for a birthday dinner his whole family was throwing. Andie shuffled in beside them carrying a gift bag that rustled like a paper bird, and Claire clutched her own gift, a puzzle she'd wrapped so badly it looked like it had been in a fight.

"It's not broken," Wade said, grinning. "In Chinese, the word for 'four' sounds very similar to the word for 'death,' so some buildings in East Asia skip the fourth floor."

Claire stared at the buttons. The landlord, she thought, had decided a missing button was better than a floor with bad luck all over it. She counted the buttons again, just to be sure she wasn't missing one. Five, six, seven. Nope. It was like the floor was hiding.

At the restaurant, the smells of ginger and garlic revolved around her the moment the doors opened. Wade's grandmother met them at the table and pressed a small red envelope into each of their hands. Claire had brought money for a gift card, but Wade shook his head quickly behind his grandmother's back and mouthed, "Not money tonight." She slid the envelope, unopened, into her pocket and decided she'd ask later, because clearly there were rules here she didn't know yet.

Dinner was a lesson in itself. Wade's little brother reached across the whole table for the sweet and sour pork, and his aunt tapped his chopsticks with hers like a fencing match. Claire, watching, kept her elbows in and waited until dishes were passed her way. When the tea got low, she refilled the grandmother's cup before her own, because she'd noticed everyone doing that, and the grandmother patted her hand so warmly Claire glowed.

Later, over cake, Andie told the story of the elevator, waving her fork. "So technically we're on the fifth floor, but really we're on the fourth. It's a whole fake floor." Wade's brother immediately announced he lived on a secret floor and planned to revolve around it, spinning in his chair until he got dizzy and had to stop.

"You didn't open your envelope," Wade whispered to Claire as they cleared plates.

"I didn't want to get it wrong," she whispered back.

"Grandma says you keep it. That's the custom. Open it later, not in front of her."

At home, Claire peeled it open and found a crisp two-dollar bill and a note in wobbly handwriting: Come again. She stuck it above her desk, next to the puzzle receipt, and made a plan to learn five words of Chinese before the next birthday, starting with whatever "four" was, since that one was clearly powerful.

She texted Wade: Next time I press the secret button.

He replied with a single eggplant emoji, which she decided was toxic, and she laughed all the way down the hall.

activity: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
knowledge_domain: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
fact: In both 1995 and 1996 David Justice had a higher batting average than Derek Jeter, yet Jeter's average for the two years combined was higher.
story:
Penelope found the note taped inside her desk on Monday morning, folded into a lopsided triangle the way Emilio always folded them. "Meet me in the computer lab at lunch," it read. "I need you to supervise something. Bring your brain. It's urgent." Emilio's urgent usually meant a lost pencil, but he had been talking about the baseball stats club all week, so she went.

The lab smelled like warm keyboards. Emilio was already there, hunched over a screen, clicking through old player pages. "I'm making a case to Mr. Bondarenko," he said. "The club picks a greatest player of the nineties at the end of the term, and I'm going to win the argument with David Justice. Look. In 1995 he beat Derek Jeter, and in 1996 he beat him again. Justice has the higher batting average both years. Two seasons, two wins. Done." He leaned back with his arms crossed, sure of himself.

Penelope pulled up the second chair. She believed in checking things, the way she believed in checking her answers in math before handing anything in. "So put both years together," she said. "Then the case is closed forever." She started copying numbers into her notebook, which was tedious work, row after row of digits, and behind them she could hear Mr. Bondarenko's class next door reciting vocabulary for their science quiz, someone saying "herbivore" twice because they stuttered on the h.

The room got quiet while she added the columns. Emilio stopped tapping his foot. Outside, a coach blew a whistle three times, and neither of them looked up.

"Wait," Penelope said.

"What do you mean, wait?"

"Look at this." She turned the notebook toward him. She had combined the two seasons, and the numbers had flipped. Jeter's combined average for 1995 and 1996 was higher than Justice's. She checked it twice, then a third time, because it could not be right, except that it was. One player could win each season and still lose when the seasons were put together.

Emilio stared at the screen for a long moment. Then he grabbed a fresh sheet of paper and began folding it into one of his lopsided triangles. "Mr. Bondarenko needs to see this," he said. "Forget the argument. Forget winning. This is better." He wrote on the outside of the triangle in big letters: OPEN THIS FIRST. Then he was out the door and halfway down the hallway, shouting, "Mr. Bondarenko! Mr. Bondarenko, wait till you see what the numbers did!"

activity: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
knowledge_domain: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
fact: In experiments by psychologist Henri Tajfel, people favoured members of their own group even when the groups had been assigned completely at random.
story:
Edouard had come to the spring cultural festival with one plan: eat his grandmother's samosas, watch the dancers, and find the booth with the honey cake. But near the fountain, a volunteer in a green sash was handing out wristbands from a shoebox, and the wristbands were the price of admission to the tasting contest. "Close your eyes and pick," she said. Edouard reached in and pulled out a translucent blue band, thin enough to see his skin through.

"Blue," said Zackery, holding up his own. "Me too." Lily-Rose drew red, and her shoulders dropped. "Half my cake samples just walked away," she said, and drifted toward the red tent.

The contest worked like this: the tasting tables were split by colour, and the crowd voted by dropping pebbles in jars. Edouard soon noticed something strange. The blue tent was cheering for a plate of dumplings that, honestly, tasted like cardboard. He had tried one. The red tent was cheering just as loudly for a tray of burnt rice. He tested his idea quietly, the way he tested things: he walked to the red jar and dropped a pebble in for the blue dumplings, then stood back to listen.

"Traitor," someone behind him muttered, though not angrily. A man in a blue band pointed at the red tent and said, "We'll crush them." Edouard frowned. Nobody had chosen their colour. The bands had come out of a shoebox. He found Lily-Rose by the lemonade stand and asked, "Why does everyone care so much about a random wristband?"

She licked sugar off her thumb. "My mom studied this in university. A psychologist named Henri Tajfel did experiments where people favoured their own group even when the groups had been assigned completely at random." She shrugged. "The bands, yeah. Exactly like that."

Edouard looked back at the two tents. The blue group had started a clapping ritual, three claps and a shout, and the red group had answered with a stomping beat. Neither group had existed an hour ago, and now they had hand signals and battle songs. He tried one more test: he turned his band inside out, so the white lining showed, and walked between the tents. The cheering did not stop for him. Nobody cheered for plain white.

Ms. Berg, his neighbour, was selling bread at a small table between the tents, outside both colours. He bought a roll and told her what he had noticed. She nodded and flipped a pebble into the red jar, then the blue jar, one for each. "My grandmother came from a place that had too much of this," she said. "I vote for both." Edouard ate his roll slowly, watching the jars fill. Then he turned his band back to blue, walked to the red tent, and held out his hand to Lily-Rose. "Save me a piece of that burnt rice," he said. "I want to taste what you're cheering about."

activity: performing on stage for the first time in a school concert
knowledge_domain: performing on stage for the first time in a school concert
fact: Upstage is the back of the stage, farthest from the audience, and downstage is the front, nearest the audience.
story:
Grace stood in the dressing room with her sneakers half tied, listening to the choir through the wall. Kayleigh had pinned a note to Grace's costume bag an hour ago, and Grace read it a third time before they were called. "You know more songs than you think," it said. "Also I saved you a spot next to me. Don't presume I'll keep it if you're late. Jose says hi from the percussion section." Below that, Jose had scrawled, "Duck when I hit the big drum, I always overshoot."

Backstage, the problem showed itself immediately. Ms. Asante lined the choir up and counted heads twice, because one head kept vanishing. It was the new kid, a small boy whose name Grace hadn't learned yet. Every time Ms. Asante turned around, he shuffled backward until he was behind the whole back row, nearly hidden in the curtains. Ms. Asante called it an anomaly, said she'd never seen someone drift that far in one rehearsal, and jogged off to hunt for a missing music stand. Grace had ninety seconds to fix it or the formation would be a mess on stage.

She thought about what she'd seen. The boy wasn't running away. He was walking backward, one small step at a time, the way you do when you're nervous and want the audience to be smaller. And the stage was deepest at the back, wide and dark near the curtain. That was the pattern. Grace grabbed his sleeve and walked him down toward the edge of the stage where the lights were parked. "Wait," she said. "I figured it out. Upstage is the back of the stage, farthest from the audience, and downstage is the front, nearest the audience. You keep going upstage without noticing. Stay down here with me and you can see the exit door the whole time." He looked at the door, then at her, and planted his feet.

The lights came up and the choir filed on. Grace kept one eye on her new charge and one eye on Kayleigh, who had left the promised spot open even though a tall alto tried to take it. During the second song Grace realized she'd been so busy guarding the formation that she'd forgotten to be terrified, which felt like a trick Kayleigh might have planned all along.

The small boy stayed downstage, exactly where she'd put him, and on the last note he even stepped forward for his share of the bow, quick and agile, like he'd been doing it for years. From the percussion section came one enormous drum hit, and Grace ducked. So did the whole back row, all except Jose, who waved his sticks at her over the cymbal.

fact: A heritage language is one spoken at home or in the family that differs from the main language of the wider community, and heritage speakers may speak it without reading it.
story:
The group chat had been quiet for two hours until Sarina posted a photo of a handwritten card, the script looping and dense. "My grandma wrote this for our family story project but I literally can't read any of it," she typed. "I feel like an idiot. My mom says stop saying that."

Mya stared at the photo. She had heard Sarina chat with her grandmother at the winter concert, fast and easy, both of them laughing at jokes Mya couldn't follow. So Sarina spoke the language. She just couldn't read it. Mya typed back, "Wait. Can you say the words if someone reads it to you?"

"Duh," Sarina wrote. "It's a heritage language. We speak it at home. School and everything else is English."

Mya pulled up the project sheet Mr. Mwangi had handed out and read his note again: sources could include interviews, recordings, and citations for anything written down. A citation needed a text. Sarina had a text she couldn't read and a language she could speak fine. Mya thought of a hypothetical version of the problem, like if Lisa had an old letter in Portuguese, and realized the solution was the same in every case. You didn't need the reader to be the reader.

"Call your grandma," Mya typed. "Put her on speaker. Record it. That's your source."

"Wait that's allowed??"

"It's an interview. Interviews are allowed. Read the sheet."

Then Lisa invaded the chat with seventeen messages about her own idea, a story about her great-uncle and a stolen bicycle, and for a minute the plan got buried under arguments about whether a bicycle counted as family history. Mr. Mwangi, apparently added to the chat by someone, posted only: "Recordings count as sources. Cite them as interviews."

At seven that evening a voice note appeared in the chat. Sarina's grandmother read the card aloud, her voice slow and warm, and every so often Sarina's voice came in behind her, translating a phrase for the recording. When it ended there was one last message from Sarina: a photo of the card propped against her laptop, and underneath it, "She says my pronunciation of one word was better than my mom's."

activity: to explain how sound travels as vibrations and why it moves faster through water than air
knowledge_domain: to explain how sound travels as vibrations and why it moves faster through water than air
fact: Sound is a vibration passed from particle to particle; each particle only moves back and forth, and the particles do not travel along with the sound.
story:
Gabriella crouched at the top of the quarter pipe with her notebook balanced on her knee, because tonight was the night she finally tested her science-fair plan. Her problem was that judges loved demos you could see, and sound was invisible. Her trick was to make sound's logic visible using Eden's long synthetic slinky, the rainbow one that stretched halfway across a room.

"Watch this," she called. Eden and Kali rolled their boards over and sat on the coping. Gabriella stretched the slinky along the flat bottom of the ramp and flicked one end. A wave rolled down the coils, and the slinky snapped back into place. "Okay, so that's the sound. Now here's the crazy part. Watch one single coil. Pick one and stare at it."

Kali squinted. "The one with the ink mark?"

"That one." Gabriella flicked the end again. The wave zipped along the coils, but the marked coil only jiggled forward and backward, then stopped, right where it had been.

"It didn't go anywhere!" Eden said, popping up off the coping. "The wave went, but the coil stayed."

"Exactly. Sound is a vibration passed from particle to particle. Each particle only moves back and forth, and the particles do not travel along with the sound. The wave moves. The particles don't." Gabriella could hardly sit still. This was the part she'd gotten wrong for a whole week, until she'd taped a piece of thread to one coil and watched the thread refuse to travel.

"So why is sound faster in water?" Kali asked. "That's the judges' question, right?"

Gabriella had her answer ready, and it involved dominoes. She pulled a box from her backpack and set a line of them across the flat bottom, spaced wide. She tapped the first one. It toppled the second, then the third, and the chain crawled along the ramp, but every fallen domino ended up flat in its own spot. Then she reset them, this time packed tight, nearly touching. She tapped the first domino again and the wave crashed down the line twice as fast, each piece still just falling in place.

"Water particles are packed close, like the tight line," she said. "Air is the spaced-out one."

Kali grabbed a domino. "Do the sound part again. I want to see that marked coil stay put."

Just then Mr. Navarro, who ran the snack shack, wandered over with his broom. "You three playing dominoes on my ramp?"

"It's a science fair," Gabriella said. "Want to see sound?"

He leaned the broom against the fence. "Show me."

She stretched the slinky wide, flicked the end, and pointed at the ink-marked coil. It wobbled back and forth, and the wave raced away from it down the ramp.

Mr. Navarro bent down until his nose nearly touched the coils. "Would you look at that," he said. "Do it again."

activity: to compare a plant cell and an animal cell and name the parts only plants have
knowledge_domain: to compare a plant cell and an animal cell and name the parts only plants have
fact: Because of their rigid walls, plant cells usually have fixed, boxy shapes, while animal cells, with only a flexible membrane, are often rounded or irregular.
story:
Hannah knelt on the wooden boardwalk and squinted through the little field microscope Mr. Grant had brought for the nature trail club. Two slides sat on the platform, and she had to decide which one held leaf cells and which one held cheek cells, because Mr. Grant had mixed up his labels and refused to fix them for her. "A scientist doesn't need the label," he said, "if the evidence is right there."

Through the lens, the first slide showed cells with straight edges, like bricks laid in neat rows, every one a tidy little box. The second slide showed blobby, roundish cells, some of them squished sideways, with no corners anywhere. Hannah thought about her own cheeks. They were soft and could puff out or flatten, nothing about them was stiff. Leaves, though, held their shape even when she forgot to water the classroom plant. That felt like a clue.

"Got it," she said. "The boxy ones are the leaf, and the round blobs are the cheek." Lennox, crouched beside her, shook his head. "No way. The blobs are leaf cells. Leaves are floppy." He had been trying all afternoon to spot a painted turtle, and he wanted a quick answer so he could get back to scanning the pond. "Look again," Hannah said. "The boxy cells have walls around them, like fences. That's why they're stuck in box shapes. The blobby ones just have a stretchy outside, so they can be round or weird. Walls restrict the shape." Lennox leaned in, frowned, and then his shoulders dropped. "Fine. You're right. But if a turtle shows up, I'm gone."

Hannah flipped the cards over and checked the faded pencil marks on the backs. Leaf, boxy. Cheek, blobby. Both right. "It's kind of fundamental," she said. "If you know that one thing, you can name a slide with no label at all." Mr. Grant grinned and clipped a fresh slide onto the platform, an unlabeled one from his shirt pocket.

Hannah bent to the eyepiece. "Onion skin," she announced. "And it's not even my turn to guess." Down at the pond, Lennox suddenly pointed and whispered, "There. Turtle."

activity: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
knowledge_domain: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
fact: Grief can affect the body as well as feelings, often causing tiredness, trouble sleeping or changes in appetite.
story:
The hospital hallway smelled like disinfector and coffee, and Jake kept his eyes on the gray carpet tiles all the way to the family room. His grandmother had died two nights ago, and this was the last morning before the room was cleared out. He had not slept since Tuesday. Not one real night. He would lie there listening to the furnace, then it would be morning and his body felt like wet sand. He had eaten half a piece of toast yesterday and nothing else, and now his stomach hurt in a way that made him wonder if he was catching something. What if grief had let a real sickness in behind it, like a door left open? He turned the question over while the elevator hummed.

Abdulrahman was already sitting in the family room with his own mother, because his grandfather was on the fourth floor. Jake had not expected anyone he knew. He sat down across from him, and after a while he decided to confide in him, quietly, the way you can with someone in a hospital. "I haven't slept in four days," he said. "And I can barely eat. Do you think I'm getting sick?"

Abdulrahman tore his granola bar in half and pushed a piece across the table. "When my grandpa died last year, same thing happened to me. Tired all the time, no sleep, food tasted like cardboard. It's the grief itself. It hits your body too, not just your feelings." He shrugged. "It wears off. Slowly."

They cleared out Grandma's drawer together after lunch. She had been frugal her whole life, so Jake was not surprised to find a rubber-banded stack of greeting cards she had saved, or the pen with her name on it. What surprised him was a card at the bottom addressed to him, in her shaky handwriting, unfinished. "Dear Jake," it said, "if you can't sleep, count the reasons instead of sheep. I got to ninety-one with you in" and there it stopped, right at what would have been the climax of the list. Jake counted the reasons out loud on the drive home. He reached fourteen before he fell asleep against the window, his dad's hand resting on his shoulder the whole way.

activity: to understand the changes of puberty and why daily showers and deodorant matter
knowledge_domain: to understand the changes of puberty and why daily showers and deodorant matter
fact: Fresh sweat has almost no smell; body odor comes from bacteria on the skin breaking down sweat.
story:
The note appeared in Jeremy's locker on Tuesday, folded into a triangle like a paper football. He opened it in the hallway, away from the crowd. "Everyone can smell you after soccer. Please fix it. A friend." His ears went hot. He read it twice, then crumpled it into his pocket before anyone could see.

At lunch he sat with Maxine and Marina and said nothing about the note. He was thinking too hard to talk. After Saturday's game in the heat, Maxine had announced that sweat itself stinks, and Marina had laughed and said no, sweat doesn't stink, but she wouldn't say what did. Jeremy had even done an experiment of his own. He'd wiped sweat off his forearm with a clean towel right after running, sniffed it, and found almost no smell at all. His shirt later, though, was a different story. Something invisible was going on. Sweat was the innocent part, he was almost sure of it, and something else did the damage later.

"You look like a detective," Maxine said, waving a fry at him.

"I'm figuring something out," he said. "Meet me at the pharmacy after school. Both of you."

Ms. Patel, the pharmacist, raised an eyebrow at three eleven-year-olds marching to the deodorant aisle like they were founding a dynasty of hygiene, as Maxine put it. Jeremy studied the shelves. One label had a weird cartoon skunk wearing sunglasses, so eccentric that Marina giggled and took a picture of it.

"Okay," Jeremy said, holding up two sticks of deodorant like evidence. "Saturday you said sweat stinks. But I tested it. Fresh sweat off my arm had almost no smell."

"So?" Maxine crossed her arms.

"So the smell shows up later. It's not the sweat itself." He picked up a bottle labeled antibacterial body wash and turned it slowly in his hand, watching them both. "Bacteria on the skin break down the sweat. That's where the smell comes from. That's why washing every day matters, and why this stuff works."

Marina grinned. "That's what I was trying to tell you, Maxine."

"You could have just said it," Maxine muttered.

At the counter, Jeremy counted out his allowance for the deodorant and the body wash. Ms. Patel rang it up, then leaned over the counter. "Daily shower, every single day, not just when you remember. Got it?"

"Got it," Jeremy said. He slid the crumpled note across the counter so she could see it, then folded it back into his pocket, a mystery solved, a clue kept.

Maxine held the door open. "Same time Saturday?"

"Same time," Jeremy said, and dropped the deodorant into his backpack with the note.

activity: to understand the changes of puberty and why daily showers and deodorant matter
knowledge_domain: to understand the changes of puberty and why daily showers and deodorant matter
fact: During puberty, sweat glands in the armpits and groin called apocrine glands become active and start producing sweat.
story:
Noah yanked his gym shirt out of his backpack at Grandpa's house and held it at arm's length. Last year his shirts never smelled like this. He sniffed the collar, then the hem, then, carefully, each armpit. The stink lived in the armpits only, which was weird, because his arms barely sweated at all.

"Grandpa, do you have two clothespins?" he called from the laundry room. He clipped the pins over his nose for one sniff, then moved them so each pin isolated one nostril, sniffing the collar with one side of his nose and the armpit with the other. Science, sort of. The armpit side lost. Badly. He was still experimenting when his phone buzzed with a message from Bodhi, who was home recovering from a concussion he got at hockey practice and had been reading his older sister's health textbook out of boredom. Noah read it out loud to the room:

"Dear Noah, you will not believe this. During puberty, sweat glands in the armpits and groin, called apocrine glands, become active and start producing sweat. APOCRINE. It's a real word, I checked twice. So your shirt smells because those glands turned on, like a switch. Also my head is fine, I can come to Grandpa's on Saturday if the doctor says yes. Bring the good snacks."

Noah read it twice, grinning. A hidden switch in his own body, flipped this year and never last year. That meant the fix had to happen where the glands were, every single day, not just when he felt sweaty.

"Apocrine," he said out loud, just to hear it. "Grandpa, can I do laundry here? I'm starting a whole new system."

Grandpa laughed from the kitchen. "Soap's under the sink, and there's a fresh stick of deodorant in the bathroom cabinet, never opened. Help yourself."

Noah stuffed the shirt in the washer, poured the soap, and marched upstairs to claim the deodorant before anyone else could. Then he texted back: "Saturday YES. Bring your sister's book."

activity: to mediate an argument between two friends without taking a side
knowledge_domain: to mediate an argument between two friends without taking a side
fact: A "position" is what someone demands, while an "interest" is the reason they want it; people with clashing positions often have interests that could both be met.
story:
The argument started over a plastic spoon, which Hazel thought was bizarre until she heard what came with it. Cale and Michel both wanted to be the conductor for the party game where everyone got a noisemaker and one person stood at the front waving a wooden spoon like a baton. Michel had grabbed the spoon first, and Cale was now holding the other end of it, and neither of them was letting go.

"You always get to be in charge," Cale said. "Give it."

"You don't even want to conduct," Michel said. "You just want to stand where everyone can see you."

Ms. Kobayashi, whose backyard it was, caught Hazel's eye and then went back to slicing the cake, which Hazel understood to mean: your problem. Great. She took a breath and stepped between them.

"Wait," she said. "Cale, why do you want the spoon?"

"Because it's my turn to be in charge." That was what Cale demanded, his position, but it wasn't a reason. So Hazel tried again, asking why being in charge mattered, and the answer came out sideways: Cale's little brother always bossed him around at home, and at this party he wanted one hour where somebody wasn't telling him what to do. Michel's answer came out faster. He had practiced conducting with his headphones on all week, and if he didn't do it now, in front of people, he would lose his nerve.

Hazel stood there holding her cupcake and thinking. She remembered a line from a poster in the library: positions are what you demand, interests are why you want it. Two people could demand the same thing for completely different reasons. The spoon was the position. The reasons underneath were the interests. She looked at both of them and realized the reasons didn't actually collide, if she could get them to revise the plan a little.

"Michel conducts first," she said. "Cale gets to make up the rules for the song, anything he wants, and Michel has to conduct whatever Cale invents. Silly rules, weird rules, all of it. Then you switch for round two."

"Any rules?" Cale said, and a grin started at the corners of his mouth.

"Even a rule that everyone has to hop on one foot," Michel said. He handed over a slip of paper from his pocket, where he had already scribbled a conducting pattern. "As long as they follow this."

Cale took the paper, studied it, and announced that the first rule was that Michel had to conduct while balancing on one leg. Michel laughed so hard he almost dropped the spoon, then hopped up onto the low garden wall and raised it high. "Ready," he called out. "One and two and hop!"

activity: to create a strong password and explain why the same one should not be reused
