fact: Two-factor authentication asks for a second proof, such as a code sent to a phone, so a stolen password on its own is not enough to log in.
story:
Matteo flopped onto the living room couch with the family laptop and a granola bar, because tonight he was going to beat the login screen once and for all. His school had sent home a note saying every student needed a new password for the class portal, and Ms. Goh had written "make it strong" in red pen at the bottom, as if that explained anything. He typed "matteo123" and stared at the little bar that turned red, then orange, like the laptop was personally disappointed in him.

He called Erica, who showed up ten minutes later with Vicky trailing behind her, drawn by the promise of leftover granola bars. "You need a passphrase, not a password," Erica said, plopping onto the cushion beside him. "Like, four random words. My dad uses one about agriculture, because he says nobody guesses farming words." Vicky snickered. "Nobody guesses farming words because nobody wants to." Matteo typed "purple-tapir-cactus-soup" and watched the bar flourish into a deep, satisfied green. He felt like he'd won something. Then he did what he always did: he opened a notebook and wrote the new password down next to his old ones, and Vicky leaned over and read them aloud in a game-show voice, which was exactly the moment he understood the problem.

"Every site has the same one," he said slowly. "Look. Gaming site, cartoon site, this portal. All matteo123." He remembered, in a flash, the afternoon last spring when his points had vanished from the basketball game and the coach's son had shrugged and said someone "must have guessed it." Matteo had blamed his little cousin. His little cousin had been innocent, which Matteo now admitted, at least silently, and the real culprit had probably been the password itself, reused everywhere like a single key for the whole neighborhood. He went down the list, site by site, and gave each one its own four random words, working so fast Erica had to grab the granola box to safety.

Then the twist arrived. On the cartoon site, after he changed the password, a message popped up: someone had just tried to log in from another country. His stomach dropped. "It's the thief," Vicky whispered, delighted and horrified at once. But before either of them could panic, the screen asked for a code, one sent to his mom's phone. "Two-factor authentication," Erica said. "It wants a second proof." The code request sat there, blocking the stranger like a bouncer at a door, and Matteo realized the stolen password alone was useless now. He'd gotten something wrong and it had still turned out fine, which felt almost like cheating.

His mom's phone buzzed from the kitchen. She called out, "Matteo, why is there a code on my phone?" He grinned at the two of them and called back, "It's a long story! It involves a purple tapir!"

activity: to revise a draft by cutting weak adjectives and varying sentence length
knowledge_domain: to revise a draft by cutting weak adjectives and varying sentence length
fact: The Flesch Reading Ease test, created by Rudolf Flesch, scores how easy writing is to read using its average sentence length and average syllables per word.
story:
Zack slid his essay draft into the library computer and clicked the readability checker, mostly because Pascal had dared him to. The score came back low, with a note that the piece was "difficult to read." That stung. He'd written about the skate park on Delancey Street with what he thought were vivid, powerful, extremely amazing descriptions.

"Mine better be easy to read," Pascal said, leaning over. "My sister's going to read it aloud at our family thing Saturday, and if she stumbles over a word, everyone will ridicule me for a month." Pascal drummed his fingers on the desk. "I need a seven out of ten. Easy. Simple."

Zack remembered a time back in fourth grade when Mr. Martínez had handed him a dictionary and said something odd. He couldn't recall the whole conversation, just the librarian holding up a page of gray text and saying, "The Flesch Reading Ease test, created by Rudolf Flesch, scores how easy writing is to read using its average sentence length and average syllables per word." At the time Zack had shrugged and gone back to comic books. Now he wondered. Average sentence length. Average syllables per word. Two things you could actually count.

He found Mr. Martínez shelving returns near the study rooms. "Can I test something?" Zack asked. Back at the computer, he counted his sentences and his long words, then tried an experiment: he cut the adjectives. Not the good ones, just the frail ones, the "very"s and "really"s that leaned on stronger words. Then he split one monster sentence into three short ones and joined two choppy ones together. He ran the checker again. The score jumped.

"So it's not magic," Zack said, staring at the number. "It's arithmetic."

"It counts syllables, dude," Pascal said, already typing his own draft. "It doesn't know your sister."

Zack read his first paragraph aloud in a whisper and grinned at how different it sounded. Then he deleted the word "extremely" and ran the test one more time.

activity: noticing the changes of growing up and puberty
knowledge_domain: noticing the changes of growing up and puberty
fact: Hormones in puberty make oil glands in the skin produce more oil, called sebum, which can clog pores and lead to acne.
story:
Layla stared at her reflection in the mirror above her dresser and poked at the red spots along her chin. Last year her face had been clear. Something had changed, and she wanted to know what. She flopped onto her bed, opened her notebook, and wrote a note for her friend Oceane, who had texted her last week about the exact same problem.

"Dear Oceane," she wrote. "Meet me Saturday. I found something at the pharmacy. Bring your allowance." She folded the note, slid it into an envelope, and set it on the windowsill where she'd see it in the morning. Then she pulled up the pharmacy website on her tablet and started a list of the face washes she remembered seeing, with their prices and the words on their labels. One label kept repeating something strange: "controls sebum." She copied the word down and underlined it twice.

On Saturday, Layla and Oceane stood in the pharmacy aisle with three bottles in their hands. "Sebum," Oceane read off the back of one. "It's the oil your skin makes. The label says hormones in puberty make the oil glands produce more of it, and that can clog pores and lead to acne." Layla turned the bottle around, thinking. So that was the hidden cause. It wasn't the pizza, and it wasn't because she'd been lazy about washing. Her body was simply producing more oil now, and the extra oil was blocking things up. "So we don't need the vigorous scrubbing wash," she said, reading a bottle that promised to blast pores clean. "Scrubbing hard might even fracture the skin, the pharmacist flyer says. We just need something that cuts the oil gently." They each bought the mild wash and split the cost.

Back in Layla's bedroom, they taped a simple chart inside her closet door: one column for washing morning and night, one for new spots. "Two weeks," Oceane said, drawing empty boxes. "Then we check." The first week, two new pimples appeared anyway, and Layla almost quit, but she kept washing, twice a day, gentle and steady. By the end of the second week the chart showed almost nothing new, and the old spots were fading. Layla drew a small star in the corner of the chart to preserve the moment, then held the marker out to Oceane. "Your turn to start a chart," she said. "I'll buy the next bottle."

activity: going on a family trip away from home
knowledge_domain: going on a family trip away from home
fact: Yellowstone became the first national park in the United States on March 1, 1872, when President Ulysses S. Grant signed it into law.
story:
The departures board flicked to ON TIME just as Norah's dad handed out the boarding passes, and she grabbed hers like a golden ticket. Gate B14, Yellowstone, five days of geysers and bison. The only problem was the crossword puzzle her seatmate Carl had assigned her, because Carl was flying to the same park with his own family and had declared a vacation-long trivia war. One clue had stumped her on the walk through security: "First U.S. national park, two words." Her answer sheet said "vague" next to it, which was her code for no idea.

Waiting at the gate, Norah stared at the clue. She couldn't see the answer anywhere, but she could test an idea about it. Maybe the park itself dropped hints, like a pattern hiding in plain sight. She pulled the park brochure from her backpack and skimmed every paragraph, hunting for anything old, anything official, anything with a date. She flipped it over twice, convinced the answer had to be printed somewhere, because parks loved bragging about themselves.

Then Remington, from their class, plopped into the seat beside her with a giant pretzel. "Sitting behind you on the plane," she announced. "My mom says sorry in advance for my little brother." She leaned over. "What are you scribbling?"

"Crossword war with Carl," Norah said. "I'm missing the Yellowstone clue."

Remington's eyes went huge. "My grandpa quizzes us on that every single trip. He says a ranger stumped our whole family at a campfire talk with the same question." She lowered her voice like it was a secret code. "Yellowstone became the first national park in the United States on March 1, 1872, when President Ulysses S. Grant signed it into law."

Norah wrote it down at top speed. "Remington, you just won me the war."

"Boarding Group Two," the gate agent called, and Norah shot up so fast she nearly dropped the brochure. A strap on her backpack snagged the armrest, trying to hinder her, but she yanked it free.

Carl was already in the jetway. She waved the crossword at him and shouted down the line, "Ulysses S. Grant! March first, 1872! Ask me anything!"

He groaned, and half the line laughed.

activity: to understand the changes of puberty and why daily showers and deodorant matter
knowledge_domain: to understand the changes of puberty and why daily showers and deodorant matter
fact: Antiperspirants reduce sweating by using aluminum compounds that temporarily plug the sweat ducts.
story:
Zoey stood in the gym changeroom holding her shirt sleeve away from her armpit, sniffing cautiously, and wished she hadn't. After gym she smelled like the hallway near the cafeteria on a hot day. Jenson noticed too, because at lunch he slid his desk a few inches away, and Karim whispered, "It's not just you. Half the class smells after dodgeball." That made Zoey feel slightly better, but only slightly. She wanted to fix it, not just survive it.

In Ms. Nowak's health class there was a basket on the shelf labeled "take one if you need one," filled with two kinds of sticks. One said deodorant. The other said antiperspirant, and in smaller letters, aluminum compounds. Zoey took one of each and turned them over. Karim leaned across the table. "Aren't they the same thing?" Ms. Nowak, who enforced the no-talking rule during reading time, was busy at her desk, so Zoey read the back panels herself, mouthing the words. The deodorant stick listed nothing about aluminum. The antiperspirant one said it reduced sweating by temporarily plugging the sweat ducts. Plugging the ducts. She looked at Karim. "They're not the same," she whispered. "This one actually plugs your sweat ducts with aluminum stuff. That's why the labels are distinct." She turned the deodorant stick over again. "And this one just covers the smell." Karim frowned. "So antiperspirant means it plugs the ducts?" Zoey nodded, and copied both labels into her notebook.

Their science project, a poster about the estuary where the river met the sea and fresh water mixed with salt, sat half-finished on the table between them, but Zoey kept thinking about her experiment. For three days she used deodorant on one arm and antiperspirant on the other, and ran laps at recess. Day one: both arms sweaty. Day two: the antiperspirant side barely damp. Day three, after dodgeball, she checked again and grinned so wide Karim asked what was wrong.

That night her mom found a note crumpled in Zoey's gym bag, written on a torn corner of the estuary poster. "Mom. Antiperspirant. The kind with aluminum. It actually works, I tested it. Can we get some? Love, Zoey." Under it she had drawn a smiley face with one wet armpit and one dry one.

The next morning, a brand-new stick sat on the counter with a sticky note in her mom's writing: "For the dry side." Zoey laughed, dropped it in her backpack, and headed for the bus.

activity: to mediate an argument between two friends without taking a side
knowledge_domain: to mediate an argument between two friends without taking a side
fact: A mediator is a neutral third person who helps two sides reach their own agreement; unlike a judge, a mediator does not decide who is right.
story:
Bentley found the note taped to his locker after last period, folded twice and written in Felicity's round, careful handwriting. "Practice, 4 o'clock. Dylan says he's right and I say I'm right and we both want YOU to decide. Bring your brain." He read it twice on the walk to the field, because being asked to decide felt like being handed something heavy with no instructions.

The argument was about the relay order. Felicity believed the fastest runner should anchor the final leg, since that position got the most attention at the finish. Dylan believed the fastest runner should lead off, to build an early gap before the other teams could respond. When Bentley jogged over, they were already orbiting the coach's clipboard like two moons around the same planet, each talking louder than the other.

"Tell her," Dylan said.

"Tell him," Felicity said.

Bentley opened his mouth to say which idea he actually thought was better, then stopped. Last spring he had picked a side in an argument between two boys on his old team, and the boy he ruled against had barely spoken to him for a month. The team's times had gotten worse during that little recession of trust, and only when the two of them finally worked it out on their own did the passes start connecting again. He didn't want a repeat of that.

"Here's the thing," Bentley said slowly. "I'm not going to announce a winner."

"Then why are you even here?" Felicity demanded.

"Because there's a difference between a judge and a mediator," Bentley said. "A mediator is a neutral third person. I help you two reach your own agreement. I don't decide who's right."

Dylan squinted at him. "So what do you actually do?"

Bentley shrugged. "I ask questions, I guess. Felicity, what happens if we lead off fast and the other teams catch up anyway?"

"Then it doesn't matter who anchored," she admitted.

"Dylan, what happens if we save our fastest for last but we're already behind by half the race?"

"Then even speed might not fix it," Dylan conceded, kicking at the grass.

They walked the course once together, arguing but quieter now, testing each idea against the track's real curves. By the water bottles they had invented a third option: Felicity would run second, where she could protect an early lead, and Dylan would anchor, which he'd secretly wanted all along.

Ms. Girma blew her whistle from across the field. "Line up!"

Felicity grinned and held out her fist, and Bentley bumped it, feeling lighter than he had all afternoon.

"So," Dylan said, jogging backward toward the start line, "same time next argument?"

activity: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
knowledge_domain: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
fact: The Internet Archive's Wayback Machine has saved more than one trillion web pages, so something deleted from a public website can sometimes still be found.
story:
The lobby filled at 7:03, and Emilia's friends' names popped up in the chat one by one. She despised the way her own username looked now, EmiliaTheBrave, because of what she had posted under it last spring on the game's public clan page: a whole paragraph in ALL CAPS about how Karina was toxic and always stealing loot. She had deleted it an hour later, but Karina had seen it, and Karina had said nothing since.

"You're on," Issa typed in the private party channel, where only the four of them could read it. Emilia joined the match and played badly, missing two easy shots, because she kept thinking about the old post. After the round ended, people hung around the lobby doing the usual things, spamming dance emotes, typing "gg" in all lowercase, arguing in the public chat about who had lagged.

"Wait," Karina typed, in public chat, so everyone in the lobby could see it. "Emilia. Did you write that thing about me and then delete it?" Emilia's hands stopped on the keyboard. Public chat meant forty strangers watching. She switched to a private message, the quiet channel, and typed, "yes. I'm sorry. Can we talk here?" Karina replied, "ask your question in public. I don't hide."

Emilia took a breath and typed in the lobby, in front of everyone: "I wrote something mean about Karina and deleted it. I'm sorry, Karina." A few people typed "oof." One typed "memoir incoming lol," which made no sense to her, and Karina typed, "ok. thanks."

Later that night, Mr. Chowdhury, her neighbour, was out watering his tomatoes when she mentioned it. "The thing is, it's deleted, but it still feels like it's floating around somewhere," she said.

"Try the Wayback Machine," he said. "The Internet Archive's Wayback Machine has saved more than one trillion web pages. Something deleted from a public website can sometimes still be found there."

She ran upstairs, opened the clan page's address, and pasted it into the Wayback Machine. A list of saved dates appeared. She clicked the one from last spring, and the page loaded, and there it was: her paragraph, in ALL CAPS, exactly as she had written it.

She screenshotted it, then opened a private message to Karina and pasted the link. "You should see this. It's the proof of what I did. Then I'm writing to the Archive to ask them to take it down." Karina's reply came in thirty seconds: "you'd really do that?" Emilia was already typing the request.

activity: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
knowledge_domain: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
fact: A message sent in a private chat can be screenshotted and shared by anyone who receives it, so a private message is only as private as the people who read it.
story:
Sofia dropped into the game lobby after school, her avatar's luminous wings glowing against the dark loading screen. Three of her friends were already there, tiny figures hopping in circles around the fountain, which for some reason gurgled like actual plumbing instead of magical water. Christine's chat bubble popped up first, all capitals: "TEAM SNOW WOLF ASSEMBLE."

"Ready," Sofia typed. She liked that the lobby had conventions everyone knew: capitals meant excitement, tildes meant silliness, and the word "gg" after a match meant you were a good sport even if you lost. It was like a secret code, except everybody in the world knew it except grandmothers.

Then a message arrived that made her stomach flip. Cayden had posted a screenshot in the lobby chat, and the screenshot was of a private message Christine had sent to Sofia two days ago: "cayden hogs the treasure chests, he took 3 of mine yesterday." Sofia stared at it. She had read that message alone, in her private chat, and now it sat there in the public lobby where Cayden and everyone could see it. So that was the rule, she realized. A private message was only as private as the people who received it, because anyone who got one could screenshot it and share it anywhere.

She tested her idea before saying anything. She messaged Christine privately: "did you know cayden had it?" Christine's reply came fast: "I sent it to ONE person. You." Sofia typed back, "that's what I thought. it traveled anyway." In the lobby, Cayden was typing, and typing, and typing, the little dots hibernating and waking over and over like a sleepy bear.

Finally his bubble appeared: "I did hog the chests. They were shiny. I'm sorry, Christine." Christine's avatar did a slow backflip. "Apology accepted. Sofia, you're on screenshot patrol forever." Sofia's wings flared bright, and she typed, "Deal. Now can we play before my wolf hibernates for real?"

activity: the idea of a hypothesis as a testable guess that an experiment can support or overturn
knowledge_domain: the idea of a hypothesis as a testable guess that an experiment can support or overturn
fact: The word hypothesis comes from ancient Greek and literally means 'putting or placing under'.
story:
The lawnmower had refused to start for three days, and Maelie refused to believe it was dead. She knelt on the oil-stained concrete of the garage workshop, one ear pressed to the engine casing while Aariz pulled the starter cord again. The machine coughed, sputtered, and died. "See?" Aariz said, wiping his hands on his jeans. "Dead." But Maelie had heard something underneath the cough, a faint sucking sound that came before it, like the mower was trying to drink and getting nothing. That sound was invisible to Aariz, but she had a guess about it.

"Your hypothesis," Jenson said, reading off the science fair checklist taped to the wall beside the pegboard. "You need one for the board." Mr. Toussaint, their neighbour, had let them use his garage and his old dictionary for the project, and the dictionary lay open on the workbench next to a jar of bolts. Maelie flipped to the H section while Jenson hunted for the word on the poster of weekly vocabulary words, the one that also had "estuary" on it because Mr. Toussaint liked to fish where the river met the sea. "Hypothesis," she read, and then read it again, slower. "It comes from ancient Greek, and it literally means 'putting or placing under.'"

"You're placing your guess under a test," Jenson said, peering over her shoulder. "Like a foundation."

Maelie didn't answer right away. She thought about last summer, when she'd let her cousin convince her the mower was out of gas without checking, and they'd pushed the heavy thing all the way to the gas station for nothing. She had envied her cousin's confidence that day, but she didn't envy being wrong. This time she would place her guess under the test and let the test decide. "My hypothesis," she said, standing up, "is that the fuel line is clogged, so no gas is getting through, and that sucking sound is the engine pulling against a blockage." Aariz wrinkled his nose. "How do you test something you can't see inside?"

"You look at what the hidden thing would cause," Maelie said. She unclamped the fuel line at the carburetor end and held it over a coffee can while Aariz pulled the cord. Nothing dripped out. Then she blew through the line, and a gritty little plug of old gum and dirt popped onto the bench. She reattached the hose, and on the next pull the mower roared to life so suddenly that Jenson jumped and knocked over the jar of bolts.

Later, painting the letters for her board, she printed the Greek meaning under her hypothesis, and underneath that she taped the actual gritty plug of dirt in a plastic bag, labeled in her careful handwriting. Mr. Toussaint leaned in the doorway, watching. "You know," he said, "your grandfather fixed things the same way, and his father before him. Almost hereditary." Maelie looked at the little gray lump behind the plastic, the hidden thing she had never seen directly but had caught anyway, and picked up the brush. "Aariz," she called, "hand me the yellow paint. The title needs to be brighter."

activity: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
knowledge_domain: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
fact: A layer of mulch, such as straw or wood chips, keeps soil moist, blocks weeds from sprouting and evens out soil temperature.
story:
Brody crouched between his two garden beds behind the garage, pressing his thumb into the dirt. In the bed with the straw he had scattered from the farmers' market, the soil was dark and damp right under the surface. In the bare bed beside it, the ground had cracked into a map of little canyons, and three tomato seedlings lay flopped over like they had given up on life. He had watered both beds the same, morning and night, turning the valve on the rain barrel exactly one half turn each time. So why did one bed look like a jungle and the other like a desert?

At school he showed Bowen a photo of the two beds on his phone. "Aliens," Bowen said immediately. "Or your dad is sneaking out and watering one of them." Brody said that theory was plausible, actually, since his dad did weird things at 6 a.m., but he doubted it. Oceanne leaned over Bowen's shoulder and frowned. "The straw one. What's different about the straw one?" That was the question Brody kept circling. The straw covered the ground. The bare bed exposed the soil straight to the hot sun, day after day. He turned that over all through math class, doodling a sun and a cloud of straw in his notebook margin until Ms. Chowdhury cleared her throat at him.

On Saturday he rode his bike to the farmers' market and found the woman who had sold him the seedlings. He bought two more tomatoes and, after standing in front of the straw bales for a long minute, a whole armful of straw. "Good choice," she said, weighing it. "Straw's called mulch once you lay it on the soil." He nodded like he'd known that, which he had not.

Back home, he tucked straw around every seedling in the cracked bed, thick as a blanket, and pulled four weeds that had sprouted in the bare soil but hadn't dared to poke through the straw bed. Then he crouched and pressed his thumb into the dirt again, right at a seedling's roots. Cool. Damp. He grinned at the tomato plant. "Don't tell the others," he said, "but you were always my favorites."

activity: to make a roux and turn it into a smooth cheese sauce without lumps
knowledge_domain: to make a roux and turn it into a smooth cheese sauce without lumps
fact: Adding the milk to a roux a little at a time while whisking lets the flour spread out evenly and helps stop lumps from forming.
story:
Lillian stood at the stove with her phone propped against the flour canister, staring at the word "roux" for the tenth time. Kelsey was coming over at six for their movie night, and Lillian had promised real mac and cheese, not the boxed kind, because Kelsey's older sister always teased them about eating like little kids. The recipe said to melt butter, stir in flour, then add milk. It made it sound easy.

She melted the butter, sprinkled in the flour, and stirred until the paste smelled toasty. Then, wanting to prioritize speed because the movie started soon, she poured all two cups of milk in at once. The mixture seized into pale little balls that refused to mix no matter how fast she whisked. She whisked until her wrist ached, and the balls just rolled around the pan like wet dough. She turned the burner off and stared at the ruined pot, and that was when Kelsey walked in, holding her own whisk like a peace offering.

"I already ruined it," Lillian said. "There's lumps everywhere."

Kelsey leaned over the pot, frowning. "My grandma makes this. She goes slow. Like, annoyingly slow." She tilted her head. "Maybe slow is the point?"

Lillian scraped the lumpy mess into a bowl and started over. This time she thought about what had happened before. When she'd dumped the milk in all at once, the flour had nowhere to go, so it had bunched up into balls. Maybe it needed room to spread out. She tested the idea: she melted the butter, stirred in the flour, and then added the milk just a splash at a time, whisking hard after every splash. Splash, whisk, smooth. Splash, whisk, smooth. Each little bit vanished into the sauce before she added the next.

"It's working," Kelsey said, hovering at her elbow. "Keep going, don't stop."

When all the milk was in, the sauce was glossy with no lumps anywhere. Lillian dropped in handfuls of cheddar, and it melted into something that actually looked like the picture. She pointed at the towel too close to the burner and said, "Move that, it's flammable." Kelsey moved it, then grinned and pulled out her phone to take a photo for her sister.

Lillian stirred one last time and held up the spoon, cheese stretching in a long ribbon off the end. "First candidate for movie night menu, approved," she said.

Kelsey was already reaching for the box of pasta. "So can we double it?"

activity: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
knowledge_domain: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
fact: A 2018 study by Jeffrey Hall of the University of Kansas found it takes about 50 hours together to turn an acquaintance into a casual friend.
story:
Hazel sat cross-legged on the porch steps with her mother's phone, scrolling through articles about making friends in a new town, because in eleven days a moving truck was going to carry everything she owned to a place called Fairview. The screen smelled faintly of the lemon cleaner her mother had used on it, and the porch boards were warm under her knees even though the evening air was cooling. Then she found it: a 2018 study by Jeffrey Hall of the University of Kansas, which found that it takes about 50 hours together to turn an acquaintance into a casual friend.

Fifty hours. She read the number twice, then did the math on the back of a seed packet. At lunch, thirty minutes a day, it would take a hundred school days. More than half a year. "That's so slow," she said out loud, and the cat, agile as ever, leapt onto the railing beside her without a sound.

She thought about last September, when Irene had been new at her school. They had eaten lunch together exactly once, and Hazel had gone home thinking they were friends, and then Irene had sat with three other girls for two weeks straight. Hazel had decided Irene was rude. Now she narrowed her eyes at the seed packet. Maybe Irene hadn't been rude at all. Maybe one lunch was simply one lunch, and nobody had told them the rules.

There was a whole controversy in the comments under the article, people arguing about whether the hours had to be face to face, but Hazel was more interested in testing it. She grabbed a notebook and wrote "FIFTY HOURS" at the top of a page. The moving boxes stacked by the door were labeled KITCHEN and BOOKS, and next week she would have to label one FRIENDS, except that friends couldn't be taped into a box.

Brandon rode his bike up the driveway before dinner, skidding to a stop in the gravel. "You seriously leaving us?"

"For real," Hazel said. "But listen." She held up the phone. "Fifty hours. That's what it takes. So when I get there, I'm keeping count. Every lunch, every walk home, every anything."

Brandon squinted at the screen. "So if I visit you for a weekend, that's like, thirty hours?"

"Depends how long you stay." She grinned and wrote his name at the top of the list anyway.

The bees were still moving between her mother's tomato blossoms, working the last light, each one pollinating as it went. Hazel added a line to the notebook: Day one, find someone who likes gardens. Then she went inside to look up whether Fairview had a community garden, notebook under her arm like something already precious.

activity: to compare the cost of borrowing money on a credit card with saving up first
knowledge_domain: to compare the cost of borrowing money on a credit card with saving up first
fact: APR stands for annual percentage rate, the yearly interest rate a lender charges on money you borrow.
story:
The remote-control car kit sat on the shelf between the paper towels and the birthday candles, priced at forty dollars, and it had sat there for three Saturdays in a row while Connor counted his money at home and got fourteen dollars. His mother pushed the cart toward the dairy aisle, and he drifted toward the checkout, where a little stand of credit card pamphlets leaned against the gum display like it was tired.

He picked one up because it was shiny and because the gum was too expensive. The front promised INSTANT APPROVAL in giant letters. On the back, in letters so small they were almost anonymous, he found the letters A, P, R.

"APR stands for annual percentage rate," Aliyah read over his shoulder. She had appeared out of nowhere, the way she did, holding a box of cereal her mom had sent her to compare with another box. "The yearly interest rate a lender charges on money you borrow. My dad reads these when he's bored."

Connor turned the pamphlet over. Nineteen percent, it said. He did the math in his head, slowly, the way his teacher liked. Forty dollars borrowed. Nineteen percent of that, added on, over a year. Almost eight extra dollars for the same car.

"So if I borrowed forty, I'd really pay, like, forty-eight," he said.

"Plus it keeps going if you're slow paying," Aliyah said, and put the pamphlet back. "My dad says that part loudly."

Connor looked at the car kit, then at the pamphlet stand, then at the car kit again, as if the two of them were arguing. His mother was now two aisles away, coordinating her coupons with what was actually on the shelves, which was her Saturday hobby.

"I get two dollars a week for taking out the recycling," he said. He counted on his fingers, which took a while because fourteen weeks needed more than ten fingers and he had to start over on the second hand. "That's the same amount of time, but I pay forty, not forty-eight."

Mr. Çelik, who bagged groceries on Saturdays and lived in the apartment upstairs from Aliyah, dropped a box of oatmeal into a bag and said, "Thirteen weeks, if your landlord of an allowance gives you a raise."

"He's not my landlord, he's my mom," Connor said.

"She is absolutely your landlord," said Aliyah.

Connor put the pamphlet back on its stand, squared it up with the others, and walked back to the car kit. He picked it up, checked the price again, and set it back down with the care of someone handling evidence.

"Thirteen weeks," he told the box. "Wait right there."

Adam had been saving his allowance for three weeks, and today he was finally going to buy a jar of Mr. Aquino's wildflower honey. He and Veer cut through the crowd at the farmers' market, past stalls of zucchini and bread, until they reached the honey table at the far corner.

A hand-lettered sign leaned against the jars: "BIG SALE, $3 A JAR." The regular price was eight dollars, and Adam knew why the table was surrounded. A woman in front of him bought six jars. A man behind her bought four. By the time Adam reached the front, the table was empty except for a smear of honey on the wood and the sign, which Mr. Aquino was now flipping face down.

"Sold out," Mr. Aquino said, sounding apologetic but not surprised. "I brought sixty jars, and they were gone in forty minutes."

Adam stared at the blank space where the jars had been. Sixty jars sounded like a lot, but at three dollars, everybody wanted them. He remembered the concert tickets Veer's older sister had tried to buy, the cheap ones that vanished while hundreds of fans got nothing. Two situations, same shape: a low price, tons of buyers, not enough to go around. He wasn't sure what to call that shape, exactly.

Veer tugged his sleeve. "Come on, Adelle's holding us a spot at the jam stall. She's been waiting since the market opened, and if the plum jam runs out she's going to be an embarrassment to us all." Veer grinned, but his voice had an edge of worry. Adelle wanted that jam for her grandmother's birthday, and there was only one small batch of it each week.

At the jam stall, the plum jam cost eleven dollars a jar, which sounded outrageous until Adam counted the jars stacked behind Adelle. There must have been eighty of them, and only a few people were buying. High price, plenty of jars, still there. He turned the two pictures over in his mind like cards. Then it clicked.

"I think there's a word for the honey thing," Adam said as they walked home, jar-less but with Adelle clutching her plum jam. "My cousin says it. When a price is kept low, more people want the thing than there are things for sale. That gap is called a shortage."

"Sounds about right," Veer said. "So next week?"

"Next week I coordinate with Adelle. She gets to the market when it opens. I get in line with her, and this time I bring eight dollars, just in case Mr. Aquino skips the sale." Adam looked back toward the empty honey table, already planning. "Either way, I'm getting my jar."

fact: Young bones generally heal faster than adult bones, so children usually spend less time in a cast than adults with a similar break.
story:
Adam sat on the bench at the edge of the soccer field, his right arm wrapped in a bright green cast, and watched Jayda take a shot at the far goal. The groundskeeper's generator hummed behind the fence, powering the scoreboard for Saturday's game, and every time Jayda scored, her victory yell was so loud that Adam caught himself grinning behind the crowd of his teammates.

"How long until it comes off?" Jayda asked, jogging over and flopping down beside him. Her breath fogged in the cold air.

"Six weeks," Adam said. "Four more to go." He tugged his sleeve down over the edge of the cast to insulate his fingers from the wind, which Jayda had told him was silly, since casts were already thick. He thought it helped anyway.

"My grandpa broke his wrist last month," Jayda said. "His cast is enormous. The doctor said he'll wear it for months." She frowned at the field. "That doesn't seem fair. He wasn't even doing anything cool. He slipped on ice."

Adam turned that over. Same kind of break, he figured, or close enough, but his was off in six weeks and his grandpa's would take months. What was different? Not the cast, not the doctor. Then it clicked. "It's because of you," he said. "Because you're a kid. Young bones heal faster than adult bones, so kids get the cast off sooner. My dad said almost the same thing when I got mine."

Jayda sat up. "So grandpa's stuck in his because he's old."

"He's not old," Adam said. "He's adult old. Different." Jayda's laugh was infectious, and even the coach looked over and smiled.

"Test it," Jayda said. "Ask Ms. Ndlovu. She broke her elbow in college."

Ms. Ndlovu was marking cones near the halfway line. Adam walked over and asked, holding up his arm. "Yours came off faster than an adult's would have," she said. "That's how it works. Adults heal slower and wear casts longer."

Adam walked back to the bench, arms spread wide like a scoreboard flashing good news. "Told you."

"Grandpa is going to hate this," Jayda said, and grinned.
